youtube.title: Why Coins Have Ridges on the Edge 🪙 #Shorts
youtube.description:
Those ridges on a coin's edge are called reeding. When coins were made of precious metal, people clipped or shaved slivers off the edges and sold the metal, then spent the lighter coin at face value. Reeded edges made clipping easy to spot. Today reeding mostly survives as tradition, as an anti-counterfeiting feature, and as a way to tell coins apart by touch, which helps blind and visually impaired people.

Subscribe to The Hidden Why for a new why every day.

sources: US Mint: reeded edges were introduced to deter clipping and shaving of gold and silver coins
Royal Mint / Isaac Newton at the Mint: milled edges against clipping; edge differences aid identification by touch
